lesson.title: From Beer Hall to Chancellery: Hitler and the Nazi Dictatorship
lesson.summary: Adolf Hitler turned a fringe nationalist party into the ruling force of Germany within a few years of the Depression, building a totalitarian state that pursued territorial expansion and the genocide of Europe's Jews.
lesson.body:
Adolf Hitler joined a small nationalist party in Munich after World War One and built it into the National Socialist German Workers' Party, known as the Nazi Party. In November 1923 he attempted to seize power in the failed Beer Hall Putsch. He served a short prison sentence, during which he wrote Mein Kampf, laying out the antisemitic and expansionist ideas that would later guide Nazi policy.

Nazi electoral support stayed marginal through most of the 1920s. As Depression era unemployment devastated Germany, however, support surged, and by 1932 the Nazi Party held more seats in the Reichstag than any other party, though still short of a majority.

President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor on January 30, 1933. A fire that destroyed the Reichstag building in late February 1933 gave the Nazis a pretext to push through emergency decrees suspending civil liberties, and the Enabling Act of March 1933 let Hitler's government rule by decree, effectively ending German democracy within weeks.

The Nazi state banned rival parties and independent unions, jailed political opponents, and moved quickly to persecute Germany's Jewish population. The Nuremberg Laws of 1935 stripped Jews of German citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews. State sponsored violence escalated further on November 9 and 10, 1938, known as Kristallnacht, when Nazi mobs across Germany destroyed Jewish owned businesses, burned synagogues, and attacked Jewish homes and families.

This persecution escalated into the Holocaust, the systematic murder of about six million European Jews, along with millions of Roma people, disabled people, political prisoners, and other groups the Nazis targeted, carried out mainly during the war years that followed through ghettos, mass shootings, and death camps. It stands as one of history's clearest examples of state organized genocide, and it deserves to be studied with honesty and care.

Hitler paired this domestic terror with an increasingly aggressive foreign policy. Germany remilitarized the Rhineland in 1936 in violation of the Versailles treaty, annexed Austria in the Anschluss of March 1938, and pressured Britain and France into the Munich Agreement of September 1938, which handed over Czechoslovakia's Sudetenland region. In March 1939, Hitler seized the rest of Czechoslovakia outright, setting the stage for the invasion of Poland and the outbreak of World War Two later that year.
